openers.information-incentives-and-contracts: Every deal has two sides, and they rarely know the same things. A used-car seller knows the car's condition; a job seeker knows her own ability; the person acting on your behalf knows whether they are really serving you. This chapter is about what happens when one side knows more than the other, and when someone may take more risk because others will bear the cost. It follows the tools people have built to narrow these gaps: rules that force disclosure, credentials that show hidden ability believably, menus of choices that draw out private information, and contracts that can never spell out every case.

nature-econ-330.title: When one side of a deal knows more
nature-econ-330.text: The person selling a used car usually knows its condition far better than the person buying it. Economists call this information asymmetry: one side of a deal has more or better information than the other. The gap hands the better-informed side extra power, and it can make trades inefficient. Distrust breeds opportunistic behavior, and in the worst case the market breaks down entirely, a form of {{ref:nature-found-045}}. The idea cuts against perfect information, a key assumption of neoclassical economics. Regulation suffers too: firms know better than regulators what they would do without the rules, which can weaken them. The main forms are {{ref:nature-econ-001}}, {{ref:nature-econ-004}} and monopolies of knowledge. George Akerlof, Michael Spence and Joseph Stiglitz shared the 2001 Nobel Prize for analyzing markets with this kind of gap.

nature-econ-004.title: Moral hazard: taking risks someone else pays for
nature-econ-004.text: Someone with theft cover from {{ref:nature-econ-805}} may be less careful about locking the car. That is moral hazard: a reason to take more risk because someone else will bear part of the cost if things go wrong. It springs from hidden actions after a deal is made, while {{ref:nature-econ-001}} comes from hidden information before it. The term goes back to 17th-century insurers. From the 1960s, starting with Ken Arrow, economists used it without any suggestion of fraud. A simple case shows the pull. Say health care costs $10 a unit and a person's demand is Q = 20 − P, where Q is the units bought and P the price. That person buys 10 units. With free cover they use 20, and the insurer pays. Bailouts work the same way, encouraging risky lending by lenders who expect to escape the full losses. Many argue moral hazard helped cause the 2008 financial crisis, through fund managers, mortgage lenders and banks seen as 'too big to fail'. Firms push back with performance-based pay, monitoring and {{ref:nature-econ-333}}.

nature-econ-005.title: When the person acting for you has goals of their own
nature-econ-005.text: Shareholders hire managers, citizens elect officials, and buyers and sellers rely on brokers. In each pair one party, the agent, acts on behalf of another, the principal, and may pursue its own goals instead. This clash is the principal–agent problem. It worsens as the two sides' goals and information drift apart, and as the principal's power to punish the agent shrinks. The losses are called agency costs. The theory emerged in the 1970s from economics and institutional theory. Its models study either moral hazard, from hidden actions, or {{ref:nature-econ-001}}, from hidden information. Contracts try to tie pay to performance through piece rates, which pay per item produced, and through share options, bonuses, promotions and profit sharing. In one study, switching from salary to piece rates raised output per worker by 44%. The problem reaches the environment too. In 1994 Jaffe and Stavins described the split between landlords and tenants as a principal–agent barrier to cost-effective energy efficiency. Common property regimes can avoid the problem, one reason their local knowledge often beats rules designed by outside experts.

nature-econ-001.title: Adverse selection: when hidden knowledge drives buyers away
nature-econ-001.text: Life insurers were the first to meet the problem. If smokers pay the same premium as non-smokers, smokers buy more cover, and the insurer's claims rise. This is adverse selection: one side of a deal knows something the other does not and uses that hidden knowledge to get a better bargain. In {{ref:nature-econ-012}}, the hidden information exists before the contract is signed; moral hazard arises after. Health cover shows the spiral. Healthy people skip it, people with existing conditions buy it, and premiums rise for everyone left. The less-informed side protects itself by pulling out, demanding different prices or staying away, so trade and competition shrink. George Akerlof's 1970 paper on used cars showed that hidden flaws can make such a market collapse. Remedies include reputation systems such as eBay's ratings, {{ref:nature-econ-333}}, warranties and lemon laws. Yet one fix can worsen another: mandatory cover against adverse selection may add to moral hazard. Even a {{ref:nature-mkt-065}} sold under a voluntary green label is exposed, since weak oversight leaves such labels open to {{ref:nature-nbs-075}}.

nature-econ-012.title: Contract theory: designing deals when one side knows more
nature-econ-012.text: A whole field traces back to a single 1937 article, 'The Nature of the Firm' by {{ref:nature-hist-049}}. Contract theory studies how people and firms design agreements with each other, usually when one side knows more than the other. Its classic problems are moral hazard, adverse selection and {{ref:nature-econ-332}}, and it looks for ways to motivate agents to act well. A leading application is designing the best pay schemes for managers. Kenneth Arrow gave the field its first formal economic treatment in the 1960s. Its models usually treat people as maximizing {{ref:nature-econ-797}} and solve for the best decisions mathematically. One branch, complete contract theory, treats firms and markets alike as contracts in which both sides foresee every future situation. It is equivalent to principal–agent theory. Oliver Hart and Bengt Holmström won the 2016 Nobel prize for the field. Holmström worked on incentives and risk; Hart worked on the gaps an unpredictable future leaves in contracts.

nature-econ-334.title: Forcing the better-informed side to speak up
nature-econ-334.text: Sometimes the side that knows more will not share it voluntarily. Mandatory information disclosure rules then require it to. In the United States, the Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Fair Disclosure requires companies to reveal material information, the facts that could sway an investor, to all investors. The rule narrowed the information gap, and the evidence showed up in lower trading costs.

nature-econ-332.title: Signalling: showing what you know in a believable way
nature-econ-332.text: A college diploma can say something a job interview cannot. Michael Spence first proposed the idea and coined its name: signalling. It is a way for the better-informed side to show its type believably to the other side, and so shrink an information gap. In Spence's example, finishing college signals to employers an ability to learn. The degree vouches for a quality the employer has no direct way to see.

nature-econ-016.title: Why a diploma can pay even if it teaches nothing
nature-econ-016.text: An employer cannot see a candidate's ability. Michael Spence's model shows how job seekers narrow that gap by earning education credentials. A signal is believable only when it costs low-quality senders more to produce or imitate than high-quality ones. Spence's key assumption follows: able workers pay less for each unit of education, in effort, time and stress as well as money. His striking result is that education can be valuable as a signal even if it makes a worker no more productive. Many equilibria, or stable outcomes, are possible. Without signals everyone would be paid the average product, the output of an average worker, so low-ability workers lose when signalling exists. The data fit the story. The 'sheepskin effect' is the wage gain from holding a diploma, beyond the return to the extra year of study. It shows up when drop-outs are compared with those who finish. Studies find signalling a statistically significant influence on wages, alongside age, sex and geography.

nature-econ-333.title: Screening: getting the other side to reveal itself
nature-econ-333.text: Signalling lets the informed side speak first. Screening flips the roles: the less-informed side gets the other to reveal private information, for example by offering a menu of choices and watching which one is picked. Joseph Stiglitz pioneered the theory of screening. Both screening and signalling resemble voluntary disclosure of information.

nature-econ-331.title: Akerlof's lemons: used cars and hidden flaws
nature-econ-331.text: In 1970 George Akerlof published a paper about used cars that brought information problems to the forefront of economic theory. In his model the seller knows a car's exact quality. The buyer knows only the chance that it is a bad car, a 'lemon'. A lemons market needs three things. Buyers cannot judge quality before buying, sellers gain by passing off bad goods as good, and sellers have no credible way to prove quality. A lack of reputation, regulation, guarantees or warranties helps produce it. Researchers still disagree on whether a lemons market actually exists in used vehicles.

nature-econ-014.title: Paying by results or by rank
nature-econ-014.text: A firm can reward each worker for what she achieves, or for how she ranks against her colleagues. The first is absolute performance pay; the second is relative. Absolute pay is widely used, but it invites cheating and leaves earnings exposed to recessions or sudden growth. Rewarding a whole group has its own flaw: some members slack while others work hard.

nature-econ-013.title: Why no contract can foresee everything
nature-econ-013.text: A complete contract would set the legal consequences of every possible state of the world. Real contracts never do, because writing one would be too hard or too costly. Oliver Hart and coauthors pioneered the theory of incomplete contracts. It studies how these gaps affect incentives, for example the incentive to spend on things that pay off only within one particular relationship. A leading application is the Grossman–Hart–Moore version of the {{ref:nature-econ-623}}. Where the parties leave gaps, the law supplies default rules to fill them.

nature-econ-017.title: Brands as a promise of quality
nature-econ-017.text: A buyer who cannot judge quality directly may trust a name instead. Firms use brand reputation to signal quality and reliability to such buyers. Certifications and third-party endorsements can make those brand claims more credible. Better information cuts the other way. One study found that information websites raised visits to unbranded sellers and cut visits to branded ones, suggesting that better information weakens the payoff from brand spending.

nature-econ-018.title: How insurers sort the careful from the risky
nature-econ-018.text: A young man is likelier to crash a car than a middle-aged woman. Screening in markets for {{ref:nature-econ-805}} means finding out how risky each customer is, and so how likely a claim is, before offering cover. Tools include background checks and demographic data. Rothschild and Stiglitz showed that even an uninformed insurer can draw out customers' risk levels by offering incentives to reveal them. Insurers can then sort customers into risk classes and offer choices. One is a higher deductible, the part of a claim the customer pays, in return for a lower premium.

nature-econ-019.title: Menus of contracts that make types sort themselves
nature-econ-019.text: A principal facing an agent with private information about its type can offer a menu of contracts, built so that different types pick different ones. In these screening models the best type usually trades as much as it would with full information, a result called 'no distortion at the top'. Other types trade less. Designing the best {{ref:nature-econ-671}} is a many-agent version of the basic screening model, and Roger Myerson and Eric Maskin pioneered these models. Applications include regulation, public procurement and price discrimination. The models have been tested in laboratory and field data.

nature-econ-008.title: Mechanism design: game theory run in reverse
nature-econ-008.text: A buyer wants to know a used car's true quality but cannot simply ask, since the seller gains by lying. Instead, the buyer can set rules that shape the seller's behavior. That is mechanism design in miniature: designing rules, called mechanisms, so that good outcomes result even when the designer cannot see people's true preferences or information. It works backwards from a desired result to a game that produces it, so it is sometimes called reverse {{ref:nature-econ-034}}. Each player holds private information, called its type, and may misreport it. The designer commits to rules that turn the reports into an allocation of goods and money transfers. Thanks to the {{ref:nature-econ-003}}, the designer need only consider mechanisms in which people report truthfully. Uses range from designing markets and voting theory to internet routing, e-commerce and the advertising sales of Facebook and Google. Leonid Hurwicz, Eric Maskin and Roger Myerson won the 2007 Nobel prize for founding the theory; William Vickrey's related work earned the 1996 prize.

nature-econ-002.title: Rules under which honesty pays
nature-econ-002.text: Suppose an insurer sells discounted cover only to high-risk clients. The scheme works only if high-risk clients gain by admitting their risk and low-risk clients lose by pretending. That property is incentive compatibility: under the rules, every participant does best for themselves by reporting their true preferences. The concept is credited to the economist Leonid Hurwicz. In its strong form, telling the truth is best whatever others do, as in a second-price sale by sealed bids. In the weaker form, it is best if everyone else is truthful. Lindahl taxes based on surveys fail the test, because people gain by misreporting how much they value a public good.

nature-econ-010.title: Gibbard–Satterthwaite: why truthful rules turn dictatorial
nature-econ-010.text: Give people three or more options, and any rule that always makes truthful reporting worthwhile must be dictatorial. A rule is dictatorial when one person always gets their most-favored outcome. This is the Gibbard–Satterthwaite theorem, an impossibility result from {{ref:nature-econ-202}}. Mechanism design can be seen as a search for ways around it, by changing the model to allow a wider range of mechanisms.

nature-econ-011.title: Myerson–Satterthwaite: when private values block efficient trade
nature-econ-011.text: Two people each privately know what a good is worth to them. The Myerson–Satterthwaite theorem, a 1983 result, shows that they cannot always trade it efficiently without risking a loss for one side. The result ranks among the most striking negative results in economics. It is a kind of mirror image of the fundamental theorems of welfare economics.

nature-econ-009.title: Revenue equivalence: when the auction format does not matter
nature-econ-009.text: Under certain conditions, a seller can stop worrying about which kind of {{ref:nature-econ-671}} to run. William Vickrey's 1961 revenue equivalence theorem shows that a large class of such sales all give the seller the same expected revenue, the best the seller can get. The conditions matter. Buyers must have independent types drawn from a continuous distribution, and the sale must go to the buyer who values the good most. To earn more, a seller must risk giving the item to a lower-valuing buyer, which usually means risking not selling it at all.

nature-econ-015.title: The standard moral hazard model: paying for output you can see
nature-econ-015.text: A principal cannot observe how hard an agent works, but can see what the agent produces. The standard moral hazard model starts there: the principal chooses a pay scheme tied to output to maximize expected profit. Such pay gives the agent incentives to act as the principal would wish. It must clear two hurdles. A participation constraint makes sure the agent accepts the deal at all. An incentive-compatibility constraint makes sure the agent prefers the intended effort. If the agent dislikes risk, such contracts are only second-best, because strong incentives rule out shielding the agent fully from risk.

nature-econ-003.title: The revelation principle: you only need truthful rules
nature-econ-003.text: Designing rules for people who might lie sounds endlessly complicated. The revelation principle cuts the task down. It says that any outcome some strategic mechanism can achieve can also be achieved by an incentive-compatible one, in which everyone simply tells the truth. So a mechanism designer need only consider games in which people truthfully report their private information. The principle comes in two versions, matching the two forms of incentive compatibility, known as dominant-strategy and Bayesian–Nash.

nature-econ-007.title: The Vickrey auction: win with the top bid, pay the second
nature-econ-007.text: In a Vickrey auction, bidders hand in sealed bids for a single item. The highest bidder wins but pays the second-highest bid, and losers pay nothing. That twist makes honesty the best policy. Second-price sales are a typical example of mechanisms in which telling the truth is dominant: it is the best move whatever anyone else does. The format is a special case of the {{ref:nature-econ-637}}.

reviews.information-incentives-and-contracts: Every entry in this chapter grows from one gap: one side of a deal knows more than the other. Hidden information before a deal produces adverse selection, as in Akerlof's used cars, while hidden actions after it produce moral hazard, as when insured people take more risk. The informed side can narrow the gap by signalling, through diplomas or brands, and the uninformed side by screening with menus of choices. Contract theory and mechanism design turn these ideas into tools, from pay tied to output to the Vickrey auction, where telling the truth is always the best move. The limits are real too, from contracts that cannot foresee every situation to theorems showing that some honest, efficient arrangements are impossible.
